extracted.intended_audience: peer reviewers / referees for Nature and Nature Portfolio journals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for scientists acting as referees for manuscripts submitted to Nature and selected Nature Portfolio journals, covering publication criteria, confidentiality, conflicts of interest, timing, anonymity, and report content. Intended to help referees produce reports that support editorial decisions and the journal's standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: The data are technically sound
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nature states it is very reluctant to disregard technical criticisms; referees' technical criticisms are taken seriously and can determine editorial decisions. Referees should identify major technical or methodological problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: The paper provides strong evidence for its conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper provides strong evidence for its conclusions
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees should assess whether the presented results support the authors' claims and whether conclusions are justified by the data and analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: The results are novel
rubrics_metrics.description: The results are novel (we do not consider abstracts and internet preprints to compromise novelty)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess novelty relative to existing literature and preprints; consider whether findings represent new knowledge rather than replication or incremental confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance to researchers in the specific field
rubrics_metrics.description: The manuscript is important to researchers in its specific field
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the work's significance within its specialized discipline — does it change understanding, methods, or open new directions for specialists?

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest to a general audience of scientists
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper will be interesting to a general audience of scientists
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate broader appeal: whether the work will engage scientists outside the immediate subfield and warrant the visibility of publication in Nature rather than a specialist journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represents an advance in understanding likely to influence thinking in the field
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, to be acceptable, a paper should represent an advance in understanding likely to influence thinking in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees should ask whether the manuscript provides conceptual or empirical advances and whether there is a clear reason the work deserves the visibility of Nature rather than a more specialist venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide editors with information to support decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The most useful reports provide the editors with the information on which a decision should be based. Setting out the arguments for and against publication is often as helpful as a direct recommendation one way or the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame reviews around evidence and argumentation rather than simple verdicts; explain strengths and weaknesses, indicate how serious problems are, and give clear rationale for any recommendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation framing — support recommendations with arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees are welcome to recommend a particular course of action, but they should bear in mind that other referees may have different views, and the editors may have to make a decision based on conflicting advice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide reasoned justification for any accept/revise/reject recommendation; avoid relying solely on a binary vote — include specifics that allow editors to weigh the report against others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to provide follow-up advice and review revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: When referees agree to review a paper, we consider this a commitment to review subsequent revisions as well. We may go back to referees for further advice, particularly where referees disagree or authors believe they have been misunderstood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to offer follow-up comments on revised manuscripts; indicate availability and be willing to respond to editor requests for clarification. Editors may not send papers back to referees if authors have not seriously attempted to address criticisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent peer review consent and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: When you accept the request to review for a journal that offers transparent peer review, you agree to have your report published alongside the main paper. Confidential reviewer comments to the editor or any other correspondence between authors and reviewers and our office will not be published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide on acceptance of transparent publication when agreeing to review; understand that only the reviewer report (not private correspondence) will be published. See journal FAQ for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent to be named in acknowledgements
rubrics_metrics.description: For those reviewers who give their consent, we will publish their names alongside the published article. In cases where authors opt in to publication of peer reviewer comments and reviewers opt in to being named, we will not link a reviewer’s name to their report unless they choose to sign their comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers may opt in or out of being named; if named, names appear alphabetically in an acknowledgement statement. Consider implications before consenting to be identified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee selection criteria and expected characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: We base our choice on many factors, including expertise, reputation, specific recommendations and our own previous experience of a referee’s characteristics. For instance, we avoid using referees who are chronically slow, careless, too harsh or too lenient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that editors select referees for expertise and reliability; being timely, careful, and appropriately critical improves chances of being invited again.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality and consultation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: We ask referees to treat the review process as strictly confidential, and not to discuss the manuscript with anyone not directly involved in the review. It is acceptable to consult with laboratory colleagues, but please identify them to the editors. Consulting with experts from outside the referee’s own laboratory may be acceptable, but please check with the editors before doing so, to avoid involving anyone who may have been excluded by the authors. Please do not upload manuscripts into generative AI tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If consulting others, disclose their involvement to the editor and seek permission for external consultations; strictly protect manuscript confidentiality and do not use unapproved AI services with manuscript content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of review
rubrics_metrics.description: We therefore ask referees to respond promptly (normally within two weeks of receiving a manuscript, although this may be either longer or shorter by prior arrangement). If referees anticipate a longer delay, we ask them to let us know so that we can keep the authors informed and, where necessary, find alternative referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept or decline invitations quickly and communicate expected delays; typical turnaround is about two weeks unless otherwise arranged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity and disclosure of identity
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not release referees’ identities to authors or to other referees, except when referees specifically ask to be identified. Before revealing their identities, referees should consider the possibility that they may be asked to comment on the criticisms of other referees; identified referees may find it more difficult to be objective in such circumstances. We ask referees not to identify themselves to authors without the editor’s knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reveal your identity to authors without consulting the editor; consider consequences of identification and follow editorial procedures if you wish to be named.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and avoidance of offensive language
rubrics_metrics.description: As a matter of policy, we do not suppress referees’ reports; any comments that were intended for the authors are transmitted, regardless of what we may think of the content. On rare occasions, we may edit a report to remove offensive language or comments that reveal confidential information about other matters. We ask referees to avoid saying anything that may cause needless offence; conversely, authors should recognize that criticisms are not necessarily unfair simply because they are expressed in robust language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write professional, constructive, and civil reports; avoid ad hominem or needlessly insulting language. Reports may be edited by editors only in exceptional cases to remove offensive or confidential content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competing interests and conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: We usually try to avoid referees who have recent or ongoing collaborations with the authors, who have commented on drafts of the manuscript, who are in direct competition to publish the same finding, who we know to have a history of dispute with the authors, or who have a financial interest in the outcome. We ask referees to draw our attention to anything that might affect their review, and to decline to review in cases where they feel unable to be objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose any potential conflicts when invited; decline if you cannot be objective. Editors recognize conflicts are not always clear-cut and will weigh disclosed information when assessing reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-review after prior reviews at other journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees who have reviewed a paper for another journal might feel that it is unfair to the authors for them to re-review it for Nature. We disagree; the fact that two journals have independently identified a particular person as well qualified to review a paper does not, in our view, decrease the validity of his or her opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable to review manuscripts you have previously reviewed for other journals; disclose prior involvement if relevant and focus on the current submission.
